A geography of form Gaps in the map Testing a round trip Meeting an obstacle

How much does
shape explain?

What is the shape of a space of possible bodies? Flow Lenia produces patterns whose forms emerge from the continual redistribution of simulated matter. We construct a synthetic morphospace from their measured geometry and use topological data analysis to investigate how the sampled forms connect and which gaps persist as we broaden the scale of comparison.

The deeper question is whether this geography tells us anything about how bodies can change. A missing form might mark a difficulty in constructing a viable body, and a route around it might offer a way to reach another organization. We test one part of that idea by taking generating rules around closed paths, then use obstacle encounters to examine changes under a fixed rule. Most apparent round-trip effects disappear under stricter controls, leaving us with a map of sampled forms whose routes still need a dynamical explanation.

01 / Describing form

A geography of possible forms

To put these bodies on a map, we give each one an address made from twelve measurements of its shape, so that forms with similar proportions become neighbors even when they come from very different systems. This is a morphospace. Alongside 25,167 Flow Lenia patterns, we place 859 snapshots of tissue developing in EmbryoMaker, a simulation of interacting cells, and measurements of 232 real fish. The map lets us look for shapes that recur across these different ways of making a body.

A cloud of matter, a set of anatomical landmarks, and a developing tissue have no obvious point-for-point correspondence. The twelve measurements below give them a common description, preserving some aspects of their organization while discarding others. The first six describe the distribution of points or matter; the remaining six describe its footprint in a 32 × 32 grid on the principal plane. Neither motion nor the generating rule enters the map.

01 / Elongation

Relative spread along the longest and second-longest axes.

02 / Directional bias

How strongly the longest axis dominates the second.

03 / Compactness

How closely matter or points gather around their center.

04 / Polarity

Imbalance between the two ends of the longest axis.

05 / Reflection symmetry

How closely the distribution matches its reflection across a principal axis.

06 / Radial evenness

How similar the distances from the center are.

07 / Component count

Number of separate connected pieces in the footprint.

08 / Largest component fraction

Share of the total mass in the largest piece.

09 / Largest component anisotropy

Directional bias within that largest piece.

10 / Coverage

Fraction of grid cells occupied by the footprint.

11 / Boundary complexity

Exposed boundary relative to the square root of occupied area.

12 / Enclosure

Number of enclosed gaps, capped at four and scaled to 0–1.

How the measurements are constructed

Distances use robustly normalized coordinates. Sparse fish landmarks are rasterized as a filled convex hull, while the Lenia fields carry mass weights; these choices affect the component and boundary measurements. Elongation and directional bias are related measurements, not independent properties. Read the coordinate definitions.

02 / The topology of the map

The shapes around the gaps

The distribution of points also lets us ask whether the sampled forms surround gaps in the morphospace. This is the question addressed by topological data analysis (TDA), which studies how a dataset is connected as the scale of observation changes. To detect these loops, we connect nearby observations and gradually increase the distance over which connections are allowed; some gaps fill quickly, while others remain enclosed across a wider range of distances. Whenever three observations are mutually connected, we fill their triangle; a loop disappears once these filled triangles span its interior. Persistent homology records the distance at which each loop appears and the distance at which it fills, and calls the difference its persistence. In this terminology, H₀ tracks connected components and H₁ tracks loops.

These are loops among sampled shapes, rather than trajectories traced by a body over time.

Largest loop persistence in each sampled cohort

The gaps suggest a question about construction: can we fill a missing region by finding more rules, or do intermediate shapes fail to sustain themselves? Those possibilities would give the same empty patch very different meanings. Persistent loops occur in all three datasets, but their lengths also depend on sampling and computation—the broad Lenia result uses a landmark approximation—so the numbers above do not rank the systems by biological complexity. They locate absences worth explaining.

03 / Testing a round trip

When the rule returns, does the body?

A loop in the morphospace is a relation among observed shapes, but it does not tell us how to move a body from one of those shapes to another. To investigate whether a round trip can leave a lasting difference, we turn to the parameters of the rule itself: change them in small steps around a closed path, let the body evolve at each step, and carry its resulting state into the next. The parameters eventually return to their starting values; the body has a history that they do not record.

This is a transport experiment. The word holonomy names the possibility that something carried around a closed path returns changed, even though the path ends where it began. Here the transported object is the simulated state, and the path lies in rule-parameter space. A nonzero change alone is insufficient evidence of such an effect, because the body also evolves while the parameters are changing. We therefore compare the loop with paths that retrace their steps and repeat the calculation with finer subdivisions.

Most candidates fail the finer test

The distinction matters across the experiment. Only one of five selected candidates from the broader collection passes both numerical criteria in the dense rerun, and none of the five checked in a separately selected 256-pattern region does. The surviving candidate warrants further refinement, but the current tests give little reproducible evidence of a path-dependent effect beyond the controls. They also do not establish that the gaps found by persistent homology have a corresponding dynamical consequence: the measured shape loops and the imposed parameter loops are different objects.

An obstacle gives us another way to ask what the shape description leaves out. Instead of changing the rule, we disturb the body’s surroundings and compare its response with an undisturbed continuation under the same rule.

Tests using either measure alone give stronger tails (p ≈ 0.008 for state closure and ≈ 0.0002 for the closure ratio), but most candidates do not pass the denser calculation.

04 / From shape to behavior

How bodies respond
to an obstacle

For this experiment we use a separate cohort from later campaigns: five bodies selected for remaining coherent while moving, including the two shown at the beginning of this article. Each body is continued from the same saved state in four branches, with its path left clear in the control branch and an obstacle placed ahead, to the left, or to the right in the others. The paired continuations allow each response to be compared with what that same body would have done without the obstacle.

  1. 626specimens replayed
  2. 184remained coherent
  3. 9also moved
  4. 5could be tested

Selection began with 626 specimens replayed for 3,600 steps: 184 retained a coherent body, nine also moved at least half a body diameter, and five qualified for clean paired encounters. All fifteen obstacle branches made contact. The chart compares each body’s median response across the three placements with its unobstructed continuation, called the sham, so that 100% would mean matching its undisturbed net displacement.

The two bodies retaining the most progress also turn least, while the others travel less and change direction more sharply. These encounters give us several outcomes to explain, even within just two related rule families. A body can lose forward motion while remaining together, or reorganize enough that following its center no longer tells the whole story.

In one placement, the body nearly reverses direction as a substantial share of its matter leaves the largest connected piece. Its material survives—the dynamics conserve it—but its organization changes. For a map meant to describe possible bodies, that raises a question of identity: should we count this as the same body moving differently, a transformed body, or the beginning of several? The answer depends on which continuing capacities we want the map to distinguish.

There is reason to expect the predictive value of shape to differ between kinds of behavior. In a separate analysis of 8,174 creatures, shape measurements explained much of the variation along an activity axis (R² = 0.725), but very little along a locomotion axis (R² = 0.038). Those descriptive regressions make it worth asking whether shape will also be unevenly informative about obstacle responses, particularly when predictions must generalize to bodies from unfamiliar rule families.

The five-body assay has not tested that relationship. It records the responses a predictive description would have to account for.

Read the protocol and all response measurements

Similar bodies may
react differently

A long body might travel, turn in place, or remain nearly still, depending on how its matter moves. Our working hypothesis is that shape captures some constraints on behavior, while the organization of flow helps determine which movements the body can sustain. That could help explain why the same shape measurements describe activity much better than locomotion. If this is right, a useful map of bodies would also tell us something about the changes each body can undergo: which disturbances it absorbs, which set it travelling, and which reorganize it into something else. Bodies that look alike could occupy different places in that map, while visibly different bodies might share a way of responding.

In active-droplet models, internal flows can stir the surrounding fluid without propelling the droplet; a change in the alignment of its active material can break the symmetry and produce motion. Flow Lenia has different equations, but this suggests a more specific question for our bodies: which arrangements of flow produce travel, and which keep matter moving without carrying the body anywhere?

Sources and analysis dates

The map and comparisons use the 19 May 2026 analysis snapshot: 25,167 Lenia observations with a common set of shape measurements. The wider collection continued to grow; a July–August database investigation records 1,363,395 creature entries. That later archive total is not the number analyzed here, nor a count of distinct body forms. The results below describe the May cohort; whether its gaps persist in the expanded collection remains an open question.

The morphology and rule-transport results come from the May 2026 analysis summarized in The Geometry of a Synthetic Morphospace, while the separate coherent-body obstacle assay was completed on 2 September 2026. This overview retains the stricter transport checks and distinguishes those earlier shape comparisons from the later response measurements.
